label: text
text: Winning by the odd goal in five from the Army at the U.S.R.C.

label: text
text: yesterday, the Royal Navy hockey team placed itself in very favourable position for capturing the Sim Shield from the Hongkong Hockey Club (holders this season).

label: text
text: Hitherto the Navy and the Army have each defeated the Club once each — by narrow margins. Then the service teams drew, giving each three points. Yesterday's victory makes the Navy's total five. They cannot be beaten. To tie, the Army must beat the Club but the Navy must also lose to the Club in the return match. Any other result will make the Navy certain winners.

label: text
text: Play yesterday was of a very high order. The first half ran evenly and the score of 2-all at half-time wins a fair indication of the game.

label: text
text: Sillitoe gave the Navy the lead. Burgess equalised. Hill put the senior service ahead again but Burgess again squared matters.

label: text
text: Some time had elapsed in the second session when Nicholson scored the winning goal.

label: paragraph_title
text: BORDER INQUIRY.

label: paragraph_title
text: VERDICT OF JUSTIFIABLE

label: text
text: JURY AND QUESTIONS

label: text
text: In the course of cross-examination by the Coroner (Mr. R. E. Lindsell) yesterday, Sub-Inspector Barnett said with reference to the two Chinese he shot near the border recently that there was no doubt but that they would have got away had he not fired. When one of the men ran down the hill he fired two shots and witness replied with two. His idea in firing was to stop them and not to kill.

label: text
text: In reply to Mr. Brayfield, foreman of the jury, witness said that he believed all three men to be armed at the time but he had reason to believe now that only one who fired at him was armed.

label: text
text: There was reason to believe from the notebooks found on the men who were shot that the latter were members of a strike picket, stated Mr. W. G. Gerrard, A.S.P., in answer to the Coroner.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE LAW.

label: text
text:
It was clear from the earliest time of the commonlaw of England, which ran in the Colony, said the"Coroner, in his summing up, that if a person whom an officer was legally attempting to arrest on a charge of felony, flees and cannot otherwise be arrested, he may be killed" and the homicide is justifiable.
The Coroner handed to the

label: text
text: The Coroner handed to the jury certain questions, and they retired to consider them.

label: text
text: The questions, in part, were:

label: text
text: (1) Had Inspector Barnett reasonable cause to believe that the three men he met on the hill-side were robber's, that was to say, felons who had robbed women?

label: text
text: (2) Did the two men who were killed flee when he attempted to intercept them?

label: text
text: (3) If they did flee, had he reasonable cause to think they were armed and might shoot him unless he fired first?

label: text
text: (4) In the circumstances did the jury consider Inspector Barnett could have effected an arrest of the men without firing?

label: paragraph_title
text: REPLIES BY THE JURY.

label: text
text: The jury were absent for a few minutes and replied to the questions as follows:—

label: text
text: (1) He had reasonable cause to believe they were robbers.

label: text
text: (3) He had cause to think they were armed.

label: text
text: (4) In the circumstances he could not have effected their arrest without violence.

label: text
text: On that evidence the Coroner returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.

label: text
text: He thanked the jury for their attention and for the time they had spent in considering a difficult case.

label: text
text: Mrs. Cook was the widow of Mr. Wyndham Francis Cook, of the drapery firm of Cook, Son, and Co., St. Paul's-churchyard, E.G., who left £1,224,381 when he died in 1905. Mrs Cook disposes of only £17,180 in her will, which is the longest on record. The total number of words is 95,940.

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: WOMAN TO USURP MAN'S PRIVITECHS?

label: text
text: COURTESY AS INSULT!

label: text
text: The alleged "unrest" among women, which signified a spirit of discontent and refractoriness, was noticeable some years before the war, since when a marked change has taken place, both remarkable and astonishing in its effect upon the nation's commerce and prosperity, (writes A. Leonard Summers, in the "Sunday Express").

label: text
text: What amounted to a desire for "advancement" of the feminine sex, so emphatically initiated by the suffragette movement, has gradually developed into an upheaval, almost a sexual revolution: The tastes, dress, manners, customs, ambitions, emotions, life, and psychology have practically reversed. Football, boxing, gabmling, and all other sports, hitherto the monopoly of the male sex, are now generally adopted everywhere in this country by women, who now openly profess to regard refinement and courtesy as signs of weakness.

label: text
text: Indeed, one polite gentleman, who foolishly imagined that the "fair" sex still appreciated courtesy, was bluntly told by a "lady" that it was not wanted, and that she considered courtesy towards her sex was an insult!

label: paragraph_title
text: REVERSING THE SEXES.

label: text
text: There is a tendency to ape male styles as regards dress in every detail, so that from appearance and deportment it is very difficult to distinguish a female from a male. Add to all this the constant penetration by women into men's spheres of activity and it becomes apparent that the ambition of the female is to usurp male privileges.

label: text
text: If we inquire into the masculine idio syncrasies we shall perceive a severe contrast, clearly revealing the other great change astounding contention that the sexes of his generation are undergoing a startling reversing process.

label: text
text: Our young men appear to be becoming almost mentally flabby; their apathy is appalling. Nothing but the eternal "sport" matters; industry and trade may go to the dogs so long as there is football and racing. Abnormal taxation, bureaucratic tyranny, unemployment, diluted beer (at high prices) — nothing rouses their resentment, it seems, whereas the mere suggestion of taxing or tampering with the Briton's been caused riots thirty years

label: text
text: What is the caus eof this extraordinary change, this deadening indifference? For some considerable time the young Englishman has been growing more and more effeminate—first observed when he began to decorate himself with rings, bracelets, etc., and bestowed undue care and attention upon his oily hair, brushing it back in what was called the "knut" fashion.

label: paragraph_title
text: FAINTING MEN.

label: text
text: Fashionable barbers declare that the modern young man spends hours at their shops, disbursing anything from three shillings to as many pounds on this wonderful make-up; That he is highly emotional we learn from the London Grand Guignol management, who stated that their "thrills" were often too much for his delicate nerves, causing fainting. "Of every ten persons who are too overcome to remain in the theatre, nine are men," we are told.

label: text
text: This unsatisfactory situation is distinctly bad for the trade, industry and progress of this country, and in my opinion the root cause of it is the feminine influence at work in our educational system. A schoolmaster says: "Several thousands of women are to-day teaching in boys' schools, with the result that 700,000 boys are being 'educated' by women. The teaching profession has been allowed to become the experimenting ground for the feminist movement of sex squabbles."

label: text
text: The present system is unnatural, obviously. Men should train the male mind, if there is to be strength of character, breadth of vision, courage, organisation, sound judgment, and other qualifications with which we expect men to be equipped.
